tracks.title: A record nobody can rewrite
tracks.text: Lesson 05 point 10 — the ledger. This one is a sub-lesson, under agents. A record nobody can rewrite. Here's the setup. You hired an agent for the long run — that was the whole pitch of the parent lesson, agents. It worked all night. And this morning there's a file… a line for every tool call it made. The command, the arguments, the output, the timestamp. It reads like a perfect record. [curious] So here's the uncomfortable question. Did it actually do what the log says? Because that file is plain text. The agent could rewrite it. A second agent could rewrite it. You could rewrite it. The ledger is the part that makes the record worth trusting.

tracks.title: A log anyone can rewrite
tracks.text: First — a log anyone can rewrite. Think about when you'd actually need this record. After a prompt injection. After a bad deploy. After a step that should never have run. That is the one moment you reach for an honest log… and it's exactly the thing anyone with file access can forge. [sighs] A log answers what happened… only if nobody touched it. And nothing about a text file enforces that. Post-incident forensics on an editable record is just theater. So the job of this lesson is to make that record trustworthy — without a blockchain, without an audit service, in about thirty lines of code.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A ledger is a seal over the run log — not a second log. The raw bytes of the steps file, folded into a SHA-256 hash chain… whose single head is signed by the tenant's identity. And it yields two checkable properties. First… tamper-evident — the log is intact. Second… attributable — it's intact, and bound to a named identity. [curious] And those two words aren't marketing. They are the exact field names the verifier hands back. A ledger doesn't store anything new about the run. It stores one number, and one signature… that together make the existing log impossible to alter without anyone noticing. [excited] That's it. That's the whole construct.

tracks.title: What gets logged — the chokepoint
tracks.text: Now — what gets logged, the chokepoint. A trustworthy record starts before any sealing. It starts with where the writing happens. And here, the log is written by the agent loop… not by the agent. Every tool call passes through one place — the chokepoint — and that place appends the line, always. The agent can't opt a step out of the record… because it never holds the pen. Nothing escapes, by construction. Every step is also time-boxed — a tool that wedges gets killed at a hundred and fifty seconds, and recorded as an error, never a silent stall. The event has the same shape everywhere. Picture one line — step, agent, tool, args, output, exit code, error, duration, and timestamp. Step is the call's index. Agent is nil for a solo agent, or the member's name in a fleet. Args and output are the call and its result. Now picture three lanes draining into one basin. The first lane is the agent loop — its own moves. The second is WebAssembly components calling through the Dock — their tool name is prefixed command. The third is instrumentation spans coming out of WASM — prefixed wasm. Different prefixes… but every line lands in the same steps file. So the seal covers all three at once. One honest note — that third lane, the spans, is built and tested, but its guest-side wiring is still an open to-do. So today the first two lanes carry the run.

tracks.title: The chain — one head for the night
tracks.text: The chain — one head for the whole night. [excited] Here's the first half of the trick, and it's transferable to anything you ever build. You fold every raw log line into a running SHA-256… and the entire history collapses into one sixty-four-character number — the head. Let me read the fold aloud. h of zero equals sha-256 of the genesis string, workbooks-ledger-v1. Then h of i equals sha-256 of… h of i-minus-one… concatenated with raw line i. And the head is the last one. Three details make it strong. First — the bytes hashed are the raw line, the file exactly as written, not a re-parse. So there's no canonicalization step to disagree about. Second — because each hash feeds the next, altering, inserting, dropping, or reordering any line changes that line's hash and every hash after it… all the way to the head. Third — the line count is checked separately. Now picture the chain as a graph. Genesis seeds h-one. Each link folds the next line in — h-one, h-two, h-three — and the run ends on a head, nine-b-three-c. Then picture a tamperer touching line two. Its hash becomes h-two-prime… which forces h-three-prime… which forces a completely different head. [excited] There is no edit that moves a line without moving the head. [chuckles] That's tamper-evidence. And it cost about thirty lines of code.

tracks.title: The signature — whose run was it
tracks.text: The signature — whose run was it. A hash proves the log is intact. It does not prove whose it is — anyone could compute a head over any file. So… sign the head with the tenant's Ed25519 identity, the did-key, and the run is bound to an identity that's self-certifying. A did-key looks like did colon key colon z-six-m-k, and then a long string. That long string is just the public key, encoded with a short codec prefix. Self-certifying means the verifier reads the public key straight out of the identity string… and checks the signature with it. No certificate authority. No registry lookup. [curious] The string is the credential. Seal the run, and you get one small file with six fields. Let me give you the verdict on it. Two fields say who and what — the did, and the head. Two more are what verification actually recomputes — the signature, and the count. The count matters because it's caught even if the head somehow matched. And the two properties stack in a deliberate order. Attributable is defined as… tamper-evident, AND the signature verifies. So a broken chain can never be attributable. There's no point asking whose a log is, once you know it's been altered. Intact first… then named.

tracks.title: Verifying a run
tracks.text: Verifying a run. Verification recomputes the chain over the current steps file, and reports two booleans. There are two surfaces. From the command line you run… w-b ledger… morning-links. And it answers — tamper-evident equals ok, attributable equals ok, count forty-seven. Now edit one byte of step twelve's output, and run it again. This time it answers — tamper-evident equals FAIL, attributable equals FAIL. Both fall together, and that's by design — attributable is tamper-evident AND the signature, so the instant the chain breaks, attribution goes with it. There's also an HTTP twin that returns the same verdict as JSON. And if a run crashed before sealing, or someone deleted the files, you get… no ledger for this run. [curious] Read that last one carefully. It is not the same as a passing check. It means absence. And absence… is the tell. So there are four outcomes worth knowing by sight. First — both ok — the log is intact and bound to its identity, a clean bill of health. Second — chain ok, but signature fails — the log is intact, but the key doesn't match the identity. A wrong or rotated key. Third — chain fails — a line changed, or was inserted, dropped, or reordered. And fourth — no ledger at all — never sealed, or the seal was deleted. Only the first is a clean pass. Everything below it is a question you now know to ask.

tracks.title: Where identity lives
tracks.text: A depth rung now — where identity lives. Skippable, but worth it. The signature is only as durable as the key behind it. Each tenant gets an Ed25519 keypair, minted once, stored under a dot-workbooks directory. The private half never enters version control — that directory is auto-gitignored, owned by one boundary so the rule can't drift. Which means a bulk git add of everything is safe — the sweep physically cannot pick up the signing key. Now the failure mode the deploy model forces you to face. Containers get wiped on every redeploy. Without a saved seed, a redeploy would mint a brand-new identity… and every prior signature would suddenly point at a key nobody holds. So the primary tenant's keypair is restored from a thirty-two-byte seed, kept as a deployment secret. Picture the boot sequence as a fork. Boot asks the environment — is the seed set? If yes… the keystore restores the exact same keypair as before. Same identity this month as last — so a run sealed weeks ago still verifies under today's key. If the seed is missing… boot mints a fresh keypair. The old ledgers stay tamper-evident — the chain still checks — but attributable now binds them to a key no one holds. So set the secret, and the whole history stays signed by one continuous identity. One caveat — only the primary tenant is restored this way today. Others regenerate on redeploy until bring-your-own-key storage lands.

tracks.title: One key, two rails
tracks.text: Another depth rung — one key, two rails. The did-key that signs runs is not single-purpose. The very same key also signs published artifacts — a manifest over a workbook's canonical JSON, embedded right in the published HTML, and verifiable with w-b verify. So… one identity, two rails. Run provenance… and artifact provenance. Here's the verdict on how they differ. The manifest rail is the portable one — a signed workbook carries its proof inside itself, and w-b verify checks it anywhere. The ledger rail is not yet portable — verifying a run still needs access to the workdir files. And there's a quiet third power — the same identity maps to an X25519 key, so encrypted content keys can be wrapped to it. But that map isn't yet checked against the reference vectors, so key release stays escrow-only for now. One keypair, three powers. Sign runs… sign artifacts… receive encrypted keys.

tracks.title: Private by default, public by anchor
tracks.text: Private by default, public by anchor. Here's something important — by default, the ledger never leaves home. The steps file, the status and trace files, the telemetry, AND the ledger file itself… are all session-private. Never committed, never bundled, never shipped. The rule the whole system holds — sharing exposes the work… never the session that produced it. So the seal exists, and proves the run, without anyone outside ever seeing it. Making the head public is a separate, explicit act — anchoring. Picture a deliberate door. On the left, the workdir holds the steps and the sealed ledger — both private. The single arrow is anchoring — an opt-in act that copies the head into the tenant's git repo on the right… where git's own content-addressing witnesses it, outside the workdir, where the agent can't reach it. One honest caveat. Anchoring beyond git — to an external record — is the planned next leg. And the anchor step isn't yet wired to run automatically. The seal is automatic… [curious] making it externally witnessed is still a choice you make.

tracks.title: What the seal does not do
tracks.text: Now the honest part — what the seal does NOT do, because the failure modes are part of understanding the guarantee. First — it's evidence, not prevention. The chain catches a rewrite. It does not stop one. Anyone with file access can still edit the steps file — they just can't do it and keep the head matching the signature. Second — the seal is end-of-run, and best-effort. It happens once, at the close of a run, and never blocks the result. So a run that crashes before sealing has no ledger at all. Third — anchoring is the unfinished leg. External verifiability is opt-in, and only partly built. Fourth — verification needs the workdir. Checking a run is a runtime operation against the files… not yet a portable offline check. Fifth — it's provenance of actions, not a transcript. The chained line carries only the first two hundred characters of each tool's output. And last… the trust root is the chokepoint. The chain proves the log wasn't changed since sealing. It cannot prove the steps were logged honestly during the run. That guarantee comes from logging living at the loop — where nothing escapes by construction. Which is exactly why the writing was never put in the agent's hands.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can the agent just delete the log and the ledger? It can — and then verify returns no ledger for this run, which is not a pass. Absence is the tell. And anchoring exists for exactly this — once the head is in git, deleting the local copy doesn't unwitness it. Why not a blockchain? Because you don't need consensus to get this property. A hash chain gives you tamper-evidence, one signature gives you attribution. [chuckles] Consensus is for strangers who don't trust each other. This is one tenant signing their own runs. What if I edit my own steps file? Verify FAILs — and that's the point. The goal is that neither the agent NOR the user can rewrite the record. Holding the key lets you sign runs… it doesn't let you alter a sealed one. Does verifying cost anything? One file read, and N hashes. Index-speed, not a service call. And — is args in the chain? Yes. The whole raw line is hashed, byte for byte. If it's in the log, it's in the chain.

tracks.title: Back up to agents
tracks.text: So that's the ledger. Not a second log — a seal over the first one. A hash chain that makes the record tamper-evident… and a signature that makes it attributable. Neither the agent nor you can quietly rewrite the night. [curious] And remember what this really is — one of the real edges around an agent. The parent lesson, agents, promised an agent's reach has hard boundaries. This is one of them, made concrete. So the way back up is short. Return to agents — for the worker whose every run this makes verifiable. Everything here… exists to make that worker's record worth trusting.
